description: Geico blamed my client for 20 percent of a wreck over three words in a recorded statement. What to do when an adjuster asks for yours.
shortAnswer: You have no duty to give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurance company. It took almost a year to get Geico to accept 100 percent responsibility, all because she agreed to record a statement and Geico twisted her words.

sections.heading: What she said, and what Geico did with it
sections.shortAnswer: She said, “I looked up,” and saw the other driver’s vehicle just before crashing into it. Geico said she was being inattentive, and it assigned her 20 percent of the blame.

sections.heading: Why the insurance company wants your statement
sections.shortAnswer: Georgia divides fault by percentages. Your own statement, offered against you, is an admission, and the hearsay rule does not keep it out. O.C.G.A. § 24-8-801(d)(2)(A).

sections.heading: When your child is the one who was hurt
sections.shortAnswer: You already blame yourself, and you do not yet know how badly your child is hurt. What you say can be used against both claims.

sections.heading: Do not let the adjuster talk to your child
sections.shortAnswer: Do not put your child on the phone with an insurance company. That goes double for a teenager.

sections.heading: Everyday words that can be twisted
sections.shortAnswer: You cannot prepare for this by choosing your words carefully. The lady in my story was telling the truth. It did not protect her.

sections.heading: You do not have to give one
sections.shortAnswer: You have no duty to give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurance company. Your own policy is a contract, and it likely has a clause requiring you to cooperate with your insurer.

sections.heading: What to say when the adjuster calls
sections.shortAnswer: “I’m not going to give a statement. Please send me what you need in writing. My lawyer will be in touch.” Do not let anyone talk you into “just a few quick questions.” That is the statement.

sections.heading: If you already gave one
sections.shortAnswer: Do not panic. A recorded statement can hurt a case without ending it. Do not give another statement to try to fix the first one.

sections.heading: What I tell parents
sections.shortAnswer: Do not give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurance company before you get advice. Do not put your child on the phone with an adjuster.

faq.q: Do I have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company in Georgia?
faq.a: You have no duty to give a recorded statement to the other side’s insurance company. You do not work for it. It does not represent you. Saying no is not rude, and it is not suspicious.

faq.q: Do I have to give a recorded statement to my own insurance company?
faq.a: Your own policy is a contract, and it likely has a clause requiring you to cooperate with your insurer. Failing to cooperate can put your own coverage at risk. If your own company asks for a recorded statement, call a lawyer first.

faq.q: Should I let an insurance adjuster talk to my teenager after a car wreck?
faq.a: Do not put your child on the phone with an insurance company. That goes double for a teenager. A teenager who has just been in a crash is scared and wants to be polite.

faq.q: What should I do if I already gave the insurance company a recorded statement?
faq.a: Do not panic. A recorded statement can hurt a case without ending it. Do not give another statement to try to fix the first one. Tell your lawyer right away, and tell your lawyer everything you remember saying.
